lessons.title: PET Bottle Production: Injection Molding and Blow Molding
lessons.body:
PET bottles start as small test-tube-shaped preforms. In Africa, most small producers buy preforms rather than making them. If you do make preforms, you need an injection molding machine. The machine heats PET resin pellets to about 280Â°C until they melt. The melted plastic is injected into a mold under high pressure (around 80-120 bar). The mold is cooled with water to about 10-15Â°C so the plastic solidifies into a preform. A typical preform for a 500ml bottle weighs 18-22 grams. The whole cycle takes 20-30 seconds. You need a chiller, a dryer for the resin (PET absorbs moisture), and a hopper. In many African cities, power cuts are common, so a generator or inverter is essential to avoid ruining a batch.

Once you have preforms, you blow them into bottles. The blow molding machine has two main parts: a preheater and a blow station. Preforms are fed into the preheater, where infrared lamps warm them to 90-120Â°C. They must be warm enough to stretch but not so hot they crystallize (turn white and weak). The warm preform is placed into a bottle mold, and a stretch rod pushes it down while high-pressure air (up to 40 bar) inflates it against the mold walls. The mold is cooled to about 5-10Â°C. The whole blow cycle takes 2-5 seconds. A small manual blow molding machine can produce 200-500 bottles per hour; automatic lines do 2,000-10,000 per hour.

In Africa, many entrepreneurs start with a semi-automatic blow molding machine from China or India. Cost ranges from $3,000 to $15,000. You also need an air compressor (high pressure, oil-free), a chiller, and a mold for each bottle design. Molds cost $500-$2,000 each. Training is critical: if the preform is too cold, the bottle will have thin spots; if too hot, it will be brittle. Practice with a pyrometer (infrared thermometer) to check preform temperature. Always keep spare heating lamps and mold parts.

Quality checks after blowing: look for uniform wall thickness (use a thickness gauge), no holes, no deformation. A simple water leak test: fill bottle with water, cap, squeeze hard. No leaks means good. Reject rate should be under 2%. With proper setup, you can produce bottles for your own water brand or sell to other water producers. Start small, learn the machine, then scale.

lessons.title: Glass Bottle Manufacturing and Handling
lessons.body:
Glass bottles are made from sand (silica), soda ash, limestone, and recycled glass (cullet). In Africa, glass bottle production is concentrated in a few large plants (e.g., in Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya). For a small water producer, buying new glass bottles is expensive and heavy. Most use returnable glass bottles, especially for carbonated drinks, but for still water, PET dominates. However, some premium water brands use glass. If you want to use glass, you will likely buy from a manufacturer.

Glass manufacturing: raw materials are mixed and melted in a furnace at 1,500-1,600Â°C. The molten glass is cut into gobs, which are formed into a parison (pre-bottle shape) by a blank mold, then blown into the final shape by compressed air in a blow mold. The bottles are then annealed (slowly cooled) to relieve stress. A typical glass bottle for water weighs 300-500 grams, compared to 20 grams for PET. That adds transport cost.

Handling glass bottles in an African context: they are reusable, typically 20-30 trips. Each trip requires washing and sanitizing. You need a bottle washer that uses hot caustic soda (2-3% NaOH at 60-80Â°C), then rinse with clean water. Inspect each bottle for cracks, chips, or scratches. A cracked bottle can burst and injure workers. Use a light box to check for cracks. Reject any bottle with visible damage.

Storage: glass bottles are heavy, so stack them no more than 5 layers high on pallets. Use crates to prevent breakage. In manual handling, workers should wear gloves and closed shoes. A fallen crate of glass bottles is a serious hazard. Also, glass bottles are slippery when wet. Keep floors dry.

Cost: new glass bottles cost $0.30-$0.80 each, while PET preforms cost $0.03-$0.08. Returnable glass requires a deposit system, which is common in Africa for soft drinks. For water, it's rare because water is cheap and glass is heavy. If you choose glass, target premium markets (hotels, restaurants) where you can charge more. Otherwise, PET is more practical for small-scale water production.

lessons.title: Plastic Resin Selection and Quality Criteria
lessons.body:
PET (polyethylene terephthalate) is the standard for water bottles. It is strong, lightweight, clear, and recyclable. In Africa, you can buy PET resin or preforms from local suppliers or import from Asia. Key grades: bottle-grade PET has an intrinsic viscosity (IV) of 0.76-0.84 dl/g. Higher IV means stronger bottle. For still water, IV 0.76-0.80 is fine. For carbonated drinks, use 0.80-0.84. If IV is too low, bottles will crack or deform.

Other plastics: HDPE (high-density polyethylene) is used for opaque bottles (e.g., milk, but not usually water). PP (polypropylene) is used for caps. PVC is not used for water bottles because it can leach chemicals. PC (polycarbonate) is used for large returnable 20L bottles, but it can contain BPA, which is banned in some countries. In Africa, PC is still common for 20L dispensers, but check local regulations.

Quality criteria for PET resin: check for moisture content (should be <0.005% before processing; if higher, dry it). Look for uniformity: pellets should be same size and color. Any yellowing means degradation. Also check for dust or foreign particles. When buying preforms, inspect: weight (should match spec, e.g., 18g for 500ml), neck finish (must fit your caps), clarity (no bubbles or black spots), and dimensions (use calipers to check neck diameter and height).

In Africa, counterfeit or recycled PET can be a problem. Some suppliers mix virgin PET with recycled PET without telling you. Recycled PET (rPET) can be used, but it must be food-grade and meet safety standards. If you use rPET, ensure it is from a reliable source and test for contaminants. A simple test: burn a small piece. Virgin PET smells sweet; recycled may smell like burnt plastic. Also, rPET may have lower IV, so adjust your blow molding settings.

Storage of resin: keep in a dry, cool place. PET absorbs moisture from air, which causes hydrolysis during melting, reducing strength. Store in sealed bags with desiccant. Use within 6 months. If you buy preforms, store them in a clean, dry area away from sunlight. Sunlight can degrade PET over time. Always buy from a supplier who provides a certificate of analysis (CoA) for IV, moisture, and color.

lessons.title: Bottle Design for Strength, Weight, and Recyclability
lessons.body:
Bottle design affects strength, cost, and recyclability. For a 500ml water bottle, typical weight is 18-22 grams. Lighter bottles (12-15g) save money but are flimsy. Heavier bottles (25g+) are stronger but cost more and create more plastic waste. In Africa, where transport is rough, a slightly heavier bottle (20-22g) is better to avoid deformation during shipping.

Key design features: the base is critical. A petaloid base (with 5-6 feet) is common for carbonated drinks, but for still water, a champagne base (rounded with a dimple) is fine. The base must be thick enough to resist internal pressure and dropping. The sidewalls should have horizontal ribs or panels to add stiffness without adding weight. The neck finish must match your cap (e.g., 28mm PCO 1881 is standard). The shoulder should be smooth to allow good material flow during blow molding.

Strength: test by drop testing. Fill a bottle with water, cap it, and drop from 1.2 meters onto concrete. It should not break or leak. Also, top-load strength: stack bottles in a crate; bottom bottles must support weight. A 500ml bottle should withstand at least 20 kg of top load. If it buckles, increase wall thickness or add ribs.

Weight reduction: use computer simulation (or trial and error) to optimize. Start with a known good design, then reduce weight by 1 gram at a time. Check for weak spots. Use a thickness gauge to measure wall thickness at 10 points. Minimum should be 0.25mm for still water. Below that, bottles may leak or collapse.

Recyclability: use mono-material PET (no PVC labels or caps that are different plastic). Caps should be HDPE or PP, but they are often not recycled with the bottle. In Africa, recycling is mostly informal. To make recycling easier, use a cap that can be removed easily, and avoid full-body shrink sleeves that interfere with recycling. Use water-soluble adhesives for labels. Also, consider using rPET in your bottles to support the circular economy. Some countries (e.g., Rwanda, Kenya) have bans on single-use plastics, so check local laws. Design for recyclability: clear PET, no colorants, no additives. If you must use color, use light blue or green, which are easier to recycle than dark colors.

lessons.title: Preform Inspection and Quality Control
lessons.body:
Preform inspection is critical because defects in preforms become defects in bottles. Inspect every batch. Start with a visual check: preforms should be clear, uniform in color, and free from black spots, bubbles, or streaks. Any discoloration (yellowing) means the resin was overheated or degraded. Reject those.

Measure dimensions: use digital calipers. Check neck finish: outer diameter of the thread, height, and thread pitch. For a 28mm PCO 1881 neck, the outer diameter should be 27.43mm Â±0.1mm. Check body diameter and overall length. A preform that is too short will produce a short bottle; too long will not fit the mold. Also check weight: a 500ml preform should weigh 18-22g. Weigh 10 preforms and average. If weight varies by more than 0.5g, the injection molding process is inconsistent.

Check the gate (the small nub at the bottom). It should be clean and centered. A long gate can cause problems in blow molding. Also check for ovality: the preform should be round. Roll it on a flat table; if it wobbles, it's oval and will cause uneven blowing.

Moisture content: if you are injection molding, test resin moisture with a moisture analyzer. If you buy preforms, you can't easily test moisture, but you can check for brittleness: bend a preform; it should flex slightly, not snap. If it snaps, it may be too dry (over-dried) or degraded.

In Africa, where supply chains can be unreliable, always inspect preforms upon delivery. Use a sampling plan: for a batch of 10,000 preforms, check 50 randomly. Accept if fewer than 2 are defective. If more, reject the batch or negotiate a discount. Keep records: date, supplier, batch number, weight, dimensions, and any defects. This helps you trace problems.

Also, store preforms properly: in sealed bags, away from sunlight, dust, and moisture. Stack boxes no more than 5 high to avoid crushing. Use FIFO (first in, first out). If preforms are dirty, rinse with clean water and dry before blowing. Never blow wet preforms; moisture causes bubbles and weak bottles.

lessons.title: Storage and Handling of Empty Bottles
lessons.body:
Empty bottles are vulnerable to contamination, deformation, and damage. Store them in a clean, dry, dust-free area. Ideally, a dedicated storeroom with walls, roof, and closed doors. In many African settings, this may be a challenge, but even a clean shipping container works. Keep bottles off the floor: use pallets or shelves at least 15cm above ground. This prevents dirt, insects, and moisture from wicking up.

Temperature: PET bottles soften at about 60Â°C. Never store them near ovens, direct sunlight, or hot equipment. In hot climates, a shaded warehouse with ventilation is fine. If bottles are stored in a truck or container, ensure they are not in direct sun. Also, avoid extreme cold? PET becomes brittle below 0Â°C, but that's rare in Africa. Still, don't store in freezers.

Humidity: high humidity can cause condensation inside bottles, leading to mold. Keep the storeroom dry. If you wash bottles before filling (which you should), dry them immediately with filtered air or let them air-dry in a clean, dust-free area. Never store wet bottles.

Handling: workers should wear clean gloves when touching bottles, especially near the neck and inside. Oils from skin can affect water taste. Use crates or boxes to move bottles; don't drag them on the floor. Stack filled or empty bottles no more than 5 layers high for PET, as bottom bottles may deform. If you stack too high, the bottom bottles can crack or become oval, causing filling problems.

Pest control: keep the storeroom free of rodents and insects. Use traps, not poison, near bottles. Also, avoid storing chemicals (cleaning agents, fuel) in the same room. Fumes can be absorbed by PET.

Inventory: use FIFO. Old bottles may become brittle over time (after 6-12 months). If you buy in bulk, use within 6 months. Inspect stored bottles before use: look for cracks, deformation, or dust. Rinse with clean water if needed. A clean bottle is the first step to safe water. In Africa, where waterborne diseases are a risk, never compromise on bottle hygiene. Train your workers on these storage rules and post them on the wall.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Bottle Manufacturing and Materials for African Bottled Water Operations

This practical reference is written for the plant manager, quality supervisor, or owner-operator runningâor preparing to runâa bottled water line in Africa. It consolidates the six lessons in this module into a single, usable field guide. The focus is commercial: every specification, table, and checklist below exists to protect your margin, your brand, and your licence to operate. In most African markets, packaging is 25â45% of the ex-factory cost of a 500 ml bottle of water. Getting bottle manufacturing and materials right is not a technical nicetyâit is the difference between a profitable plant and one that bleeds money through rejects, downtime, and recalls.

1. PET Bottle Production: Injection Molding and Blow Molding

The dominant package across Africa remains PET (polyethylene terephthalate), and for good reason: it is light, cheap to transport, food-safe, and increasingly recycled locally. Production happens in two stages.

Stage 1 â Injection molding. PET resin is dried to below 50 ppm moisture (typically 4â6 hours at 160â170 Â°C in a desiccant dryer), then melted at 270â290 Â°C and injected into a preform mold. The preform is a thick-walled test tube with a finished neck. Cycle times of 15â25 seconds are typical for a 16â24 g preform on a 48-cavity tool. The single most common African plant failure here is inadequate drying: wet resin causes hydrolysis, which shows up later as pearlescent, brittle bottles that fail drop tests.

Stage 2 â Blow molding. Preforms are reheated in an infrared oven to 95â115 Â°C, stretched mechanically by a stretch rod, and blown to the mold shape at 25â40 bar. This is the "stretch blow molding" (SBM) process. A 500 ml still-water bottle typically weighs 12â18 g; a 1.5 L bottle 22â30 g. Carbonated products need thicker walls and higher crystallinity.

2. Glass Bottle Manufacturing and Handling

Glass remains the premium choice in East and Southern Africa for sparkling water and hospitality. It is made from silica sand (SiOâ ~70%), soda ash (NaâCOâ ~15%), limestone (CaCOâ ~10%), and cullet (recycled glass). Batch is melted at 1,400â1,550 Â°C, then formed by either the blow-and-blow process (narrow-neck bottles) or press-and-blow (wide-mouth jars). Annealing in a lehr at 550â600 Â°C relieves internal stressâskip this and bottles shatter spontaneously on the shelf.

For African operations, glass's main commercial appeal is returnability. A reusable glass bottle can survive 20â30 trips if handled well. But it is heavy (a 330 ml bottle weighs 180â300 g), so transport cost per litre is 5â10Ã that of PET. Glass works best in dense urban markets with short distribution radiiâNairobi, Lagos, Johannesburg, Cairoânot for rural distribution.

3. Plastic Resin Selection and Quality Criteria

Not all PET is equal. For still water you want bottle-grade virgin PET with intrinsic viscosity (IV) of 0.76â0.84 dl/g. Lower IV means weaker bottles; higher IV is unnecessary and costly. For carbonated or hot-fill applications, use 0.80â0.85 dl/g. Recycled PET (rPET) is increasingly mandatedâSouth Africa's extended producer responsibility (EPR) rules and Kenya's 2022 single-use plastics regulations both push recycled content. rPET typically needs IV top-up and tighter drying.

Table 1. Typical PET resin quality criteria for bottled water
Parameter Still water target Carbonated target Test method
Intrinsic viscosity (IV)0.76â0.80 dl/g0.80â0.85 dl/gASTM D4603
Moisture before molding< 50 ppm< 30 ppmKarl Fischer / inline
Acetaldehyde (AA)< 3 ppm< 3 ppmASTM D4509
Color (b-value)< 3< 3Colorimeter

Pellet size2.5â3.5 mm2.5â3.5 mmSieve

Sources: PET Resin Association (PETRA) technical data; ASTM D4603, D4509; ISO 1628-5.

4. Bottle Design for Strength, Weight, and Recyclability

Design drives cost. A bottle that is 2 g heavier than necessary costs roughly USD 0.004 more in resinâmultiply by 10 million bottles a year and you have burned USD 40,000. Lightweighting is the single biggest lever on PET cost.

Three design rules:

  • Strength: Use a petaloid or champagne base for carbonated; a concave base for still water. Ribs in the body panel increase top-load resistance without adding weight.
  • Weight: Target 12â14 g for a 500 ml still-water bottle. Below 10 g, bottles dent under stacking and fail drop tests.
  • Recyclability: Avoid PVC labels, full-body sleeves, and dark pigments. Use PET-compatible labels and PP caps. Mono-material design keeps your bottle in the recycling stream and protects you from EPR penalties.
Table 2. Indicative bottle weights and top-load targets by format
Format Typical weight (g) Top-load target (N) Drop test height
330 ml still PET9â12â¥ 1501.2 m
500 ml still PET12â15â¥ 2001.2 m
1.5 L still PET22â28â¥ 2201.0 m

330 ml returnable glass180â220â¥ 8000.8 m

Sources: Industry benchmarks from PETRA and ISO 9001:2015 quality planning; drop-test values per ASTM D2463 for containers.

5. Preform Inspection and Quality Control

Preform QC is where you catch defects before they multiply into thousands of bad bottles. Inspect every batch for:

  • Neck dimensions: 28 mm PCO 1881 or 1810 finishâmeasure with go/no-go gauges.
  • Wall thickness: Ultrasonic gauge; reject any preform with > 10% variation.
  • Visual defects: Bubbles, black specks, short shots, ovality, gate blush.
  • Weight: Â±0.2 g tolerance per preform.
  • Acetaldehyde: Inline AA testing if you are running high-speed lines; AA above 3 ppm gives a "fruity" off-taste.

Keep a retained sample of every preform batch for 12 months. If a customer complains, you can trace back in hours instead of days.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HIGH-PRESSURE BLOW MOLDING AND HOT GLASS

Stretch blow molding operates at 25â40 bar (360â580 psi). A burst preform or mold failure can eject plastic fragments at lethal velocity. Never open a mold guard while the machine is pressurised. Glass furnaces run at 1,400â1,550 Â°C and molten glass causes instant third-degree burnsâPPE (face shield, aluminised apron, heat gloves) is mandatory. In African plants where ambient temperatures already exceed 35 Â°C, heat stress compounds burn risk: enforce hydration breaks, rotate staff, and never bypass interlocks to "save time." Report every near-miss. A single serious injury can shut your plant and destroy your insurance standing.

6. Storage and Handling of Empty Bottles

Empty bottles and preforms are not inert. PET absorbs moisture and odours; preforms stored in humid conditions will not blow properly. Best practice:

  • Store preforms in sealed, lined bags or lined octabins at < 50% RH and < 30 Â°C.
  • Use FIFO (first-in, first-out) stock rotationâpreforms older than 6 months may need re-drying.
  • Keep bottles off concrete floors; use pallets. Concrete wicks moisture and transfers alkalinity.
  • Cover pallets with shrink wrap or dust coversâdust and insects are a real contamination risk in open warehouses.
  • Never store near diesel, solvents, or strong-smelling chemicals. PET is a sponge for odours.
  • Stack no more than 8 pallets high for PET bottles; glass can go higher but check pallet strength.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Verify PET resin IV (0.76â0.84 dl/g) and moisture (< 50 ppm) on every delivery with a certificate of analysis.
  2. Check preform weight, neck gauge, and wall thickness at start-up and every 2 hours.
  3. Confirm dryer dew point is below â40 Â°C before running injection molding.
  4. Run a drop test and top-load test on the first 10 bottles of every production run.
  5. Inspect blow molds for wear, scratches, and cooling-channel blockages weekly.
  6. Store preforms and bottles sealed, off the floor, away from odours, and rotate FIFO.
  7. Record all QC data in a traceable log; retain samples for 12 months.
  8. Enforce PPE and machine interlocks without exceptionâno shortcuts during peak demand.

Further Reading

  • PET Resin Association (PETRA) â Technical resources on PET resin and bottle production
  • ISO 9001:2015 â Quality management systems (free overview)
  • ISO 22000:2018 â Food safety management systems
  • ASTM D4603 â Standard test method for PET intrinsic viscosity
  • UNEP â Single-use plastics roadmap (relevant to African EPR compliance)

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Bottled Water Production. Figures and tables are indicative benchmarks; always verify against your resin supplier's datasheet and your national standards body (KEBS, SABS, SON, NIS) before setting plant specifications.

quiz.q: What is the typical weight of a PET preform for a 500ml water bottle?
quiz.explanation: A standard 500ml preform weighs 18-22 grams, balancing strength and material cost.

quiz.q: What temperature range is used to heat preforms before blow molding?
quiz.explanation: Preforms are heated to 90-120Â°C so they can stretch without crystallizing.

quiz.q: Which machine part is essential for providing high-pressure air in blow molding?
quiz.explanation: The air compressor supplies high-pressure air (up to 40 bar) to inflate the preform.

quiz.q: What is the main raw material for glass bottles?
quiz.explanation: Silica sand is the primary ingredient, along with soda ash and limestone.

quiz.q: Why are glass bottles heavier than PET bottles?
options: B) Glass requires more material for strength
C) PET is lighter than glass
quiz.explanation: Glass is denser and needs more material to achieve similar strength, making it heavier.

quiz.q: What chemical is commonly used to wash returnable glass bottles?
quiz.explanation: A 2-3% caustic soda (NaOH) solution at 60-80Â°C is used for cleaning glass bottles.

quiz.q: What does IV stand for in PET resin?
quiz.explanation: Intrinsic Viscosity measures the molecular weight and strength of PET resin.

quiz.q: Which plastic is commonly used for caps on water bottles?
quiz.explanation: HDPE or PP are used for caps because they are flexible and seal well.

quiz.q: What is a key quality check for PET preforms?
quiz.explanation: All these are critical: color uniformity, weight consistency, and neck dimensions.

quiz.q: Why should PET resin be dried before injection molding?
quiz.explanation: Moisture causes hydrolysis during melting, which weakens the PET.

quiz.q: What is a petaloid base used for in bottle design?
quiz.explanation: Petaloid bases provide stability and strength for carbonated drinks under pressure.

quiz.q: What is the minimum wall thickness recommended for a still water PET bottle?
quiz.explanation: Below 0.25 mm, bottles may leak or collapse easily.

quiz.q: Why is mono-material PET preferred for recyclability?
options: B) It is easier to recycle
quiz.explanation: Mono-material PET avoids contamination and simplifies recycling.

quiz.q: What is a common defect found in preforms?
quiz.explanation: Bubbles, black spots, and ovality are all defects that affect bottle quality.

quiz.q: How should preforms be stored?
options: B) In sealed bags in a dry place
quiz.explanation: Preforms must be kept dry and away from sunlight to prevent degradation.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a light box in glass bottle inspection?
quiz.explanation: A light box illuminates cracks, chips, and scratches in glass.

quiz.q: What is the maximum stacking height for empty PET bottles?
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 5 layers can deform bottom bottles.

quiz.q: Why should empty bottles be stored off the floor?
quiz.explanation: Off-floor storage prevents dirt, insects, and moisture from reaching bottles.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature for storing PET bottles?
quiz.explanation: PET softens at 60Â°C, so store in a cool, shaded area, ideally 10-30Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the first step in blow molding a PET bottle?
quiz.explanation: The preform must be heated to 90-120Â°C before it can be blown.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a typical plastic used for water bottles?
quiz.explanation: PVC is not used for water bottles due to potential chemical leaching.

quiz.q: What does a certificate of analysis (CoA) for PET resin include?
quiz.explanation: A CoA typically reports IV, moisture, color, and other quality parameters.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove caps before recycling PET bottles?
options: A) Caps are a different plastic
quiz.explanation: Caps are often HDPE or PP, which can contaminate the PET recycling stream.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a stretch rod in blow molding?
options: B) To mechanically stretch the preform
quiz.explanation: The stretch rod pushes the preform down to ensure axial orientation and strength.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of degraded PET resin?
quiz.explanation: Degraded PET may yellow, smell, and become brittle.

quiz.q: How many times can a glass bottle typically be reused?
quiz.explanation: Returnable glass bottles can usually withstand 20-30 trips before damage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sampling size for inspecting a batch of 10,000 preforms?
quiz.explanation: A sample of 50 is practical and gives a good indication of batch quality.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid storing bottles near chemicals?
options: A) Chemicals can react with PET
quiz.explanation: Chemicals can react, fumes can taint the plastic, and there is a fire risk.

quiz.q: What is the first-in, first-out (FIFO) rule for?
options: A) To use oldest stock first
B) To use newest stock first
quiz.explanation: FIFO ensures older bottles are used before they degrade.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of PET over glass for water bottles in Africa?
quiz.explanation: PET is lighter, cheaper to transport, and less prone to breakage than glass.
